title: @angular/platform-server: Open Redirect via Protocol-Relative URLs in Server-Side Rendering (SSR) (CVE-2026-111754)
description: An open redirect vulnerability exists in @angular/platform-server when Server-Side Rendering (SSR) is enabled. The vulnerability arises from improper URL normalization allowing crafted URLs with dot-segments and multiple slashes to bypass checks and cause the server to emit a protocol-relative redirect in the HTTP Location header. This can redirect users to arbitrary external domains. Pure client-side Angular applications without SSR are not affected. The issue is fixed in versions 22.2.1, 21.2.25, and 20.3.33.
aiSummary: The vulnerability in @angular/platform-server's SSR occurs because the URL resolution logic uses resolveUrl (or parseUrl in v20) which initially rejects protocol-relative URLs starting with '//' before WHATWG URL normalization. However, URLs containing dot-segments followed by multiple slashes (e.g., '/.//evil.test') bypass this initial check. After normalization, the pathname starts with '//evil.test', which is stored and later emitted in the Location header during a redirect. Browsers interpret this as a protocol-relative redirect to an external domain. This allows unauthenticated attackers to craft URLs that bypass application-level guards and cause SSR to redirect users off-origin. The vulnerability affects SSR-enabled Angular applications with parameterized routes and reverse proxies that do not normalize or strip semicolons or dot-segments. The issue is resolved by patching resolveUrl and parseUrl to verify the normalized pathname does not start with '//' when protocol-relative URLs are disallowed.
aiImpact: An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit this vulnerability to cause Angular SSR to issue HTTP 302 redirects to arbitrary external domains. This bypasses common application-level redirect allowlists that do not account for URL normalization bypasses. The redirect can lead users to malicious sites, potentially facilitating phishing or other attacks. Pure client-side Angular applications without SSR are not vulnerable. No known exploits in the wild have been reported.
